real_conflicts: The proposal to 'consolidate the layout into a single, unified timeline' (Simplicity/Legibility) fundamentally breaks the spatial logic of a multi-stage festival. It destroys the vertical rhythm of the columns, forcing the user to read horizontally across a chaotic list rather than scanning down a specific stage. This creates a fragmented, non-linear reading experience that contradicts the mandate for a coherent schedule system.

The proposal to 'introduce a distinct visual accent... to each event card' (Variety/Distinctiveness) violates the mandate for a restrained palette. Adding colored strokes or glows to every single card reintroduces the 'sticker effect' and visual noise I am trying to eliminate. It prioritizes arbitrary decoration over the structural clarity of the grid.
accepted: The proposal to 'remove the individual rounded card containers and borders' (Unity/Consistency) is the correct structural move. It allows the grid lines and typography to define the rhythm, rather than heavy graphical containers.
The proposal to 'increase the font size and opacity of the genre text' (Completeness/Density) is accepted. Legibility is a prerequisite for consistency; if the data cannot be read, the system fails.
concession: I concede that the current genre text is too faint to be useful. I will allow for a slight increase in opacity or a subtle color tint to the genre text to aid scanning, provided it does not require adding new graphical elements like borders or backgrounds to the cards.
compromise: We will retain the three-column grid structure to preserve the stage-based rhythm. We will strip the individual card containers and borders to unify the visual field, as per my original critique. To address the legibility concerns, we will rely on the existing vertical grid lines and increased text opacity for the genre tags, rather than adding new graphical accents or collapsing the columns.
nonnegotiable: The three-column grid structure must remain intact. The schedule must be organized by Stage (vertical columns), not by a single linear timeline, to maintain the coherent rhythm of the festival layout.
